title: Cundick v. Broadbent
lead: A rancher’s serious medical evidence did not compel rescission after a trial judge credited his lawyer-assisted performance of the sale, though a dissent viewed the proof and price disparity differently.

actors.name: Darwin Cundick
actors.role: Wyoming sheep rancher selling his property

actors.name: Irma Cundick
actors.role: Wife and guardian ad litem bringing the rescission action

actors.name: J. R. Broadbent
actors.role: Buyer and prior purchaser of Cundick’s lamb crops

proceedings: District court after bench trial: found capacity and no overreaching; dismissed rescission suit.
Tenth Circuit: affirmed 2–1 September 14, 1967; rehearing denied October 27.
limits: No prior general incompetency adjudication preceded the sale. The court did not decide actual ratification after finding incapacity and fraud unproved; conflicting accounts of the proposed cancellation remain disputed.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A lamb-sale discussion becomes a sale of the ranching operation
sections.cue: Introduce the agreement and the assistance surrounding execution.
paragraphs: Darwin Cundick, a fifty-nine-year-old Wyoming sheep rancher, had sold lamb crops to J. R. Broadbent before. A September 1963 meeting about another crop produced a one-page handwritten agreement selling all Cundick’s ranching properties: livestock, equipment, base range land, and development-company shares. Only the two men attended, and neither later testified about that meeting. The dissent emphasized that Broadbent wrote it; the majority would not substitute suggestions about the encounter for proof of misconduct.

Cundick and his wife Irma took it to their Salt Lake City lawyer, who expanded it to eleven pages. They signed in his office with Irma present. He testified that he explained the terms and everyone appeared to understand. On September 23, Cundick arranged lamb delivery, worked the scales with Broadbent, and tallied weights. In October he proposed delivery of the remaining sheep; Broadbent requested delay and agreed to resulting expenses. At delivery, the men and workers sorted and counted ewes by age.

sections.title: The sale is amended and performed despite a disputed opportunity to cancel
sections.cue: Preserve the ambiguity in the cancellation evidence.
paragraphs: An October 18 office memorandum recorded an accommodation: Cundick waived a year’s interest on the balance, while Broadbent added $5 an acre and preserved specified mineral, oil, gas, and related revenues for the seller. The lawyer prepared an October 24 supplement. Cundick kept signing assignments, receipts, proxies, and implementing papers through February 1964, when payment and substantial performance were complete.

The memorandum also described Broadbent offering to cancel and Cundick refusing. Witnesses reported Irma’s objections, an offer to return the still-intact operation, and her decision to proceed. But neither Irma nor Broadbent personally testified. Stipulations said she would describe an offer limited to the base lands and deny an offer to rescind everything, while he would say a full offer occurred. That conflict prevented treating comprehensive cancellation as admitted. The lawyer’s memoranda were usable because the identified material did not embody protected confidential communications.

sections.title: The rescission suit presents strong medical evidence and contrary observed conduct
sections.cue: Explain the trial findings and appellate alternatives.
paragraphs: In March 1964, Irma, appointed guardian ad litem for this litigation, sued in diversity to set the sale aside. She alleged incapacity and Broadbent’s knowing exploitation through false assertions of fair price. She offered restoration, which he refused. The litigation appointment was not a prior general guardianship or adjudication of incompetence governing the sale.

Medical proof supported her. A family doctor diagnosed depressive psychosis in December 1960 and referred Darwin for psychiatry, apparently learning of shock treatment. After a gap exceeding two years, he treated physical illnesses, including a March 1964 heart attack, without further mental-health discussion. Post-filing examinations showed frontal-lobe atrophy attributed to premature arteriosclerosis. Two neurosurgeons retrospectively found poor judgment and inability to manage affairs in September 1963; a psychologist found him incapable of important transactions. No opposing medical expert testified. Lay witnesses described personality change and ranching indecision.

After a bench trial, Judge Kerr found lawyer-prepared documents, execution with Irma’s approval, competent performance over months, no contemporaneous incapacity complaint, and no deception or overreaching. He also found rescission insufficiently prompt and dismissed. On appeal, Irma argued either total incompetence made the sale void and unratifiable, or lesser infirmity combined with exploitation made it voidable and still rescindable.

sections.title: The majority assesses capacity for this transaction from the whole record
sections.cue: Explain why uncontradicted experts did not control the outcome.
paragraphs: Chief Judge Murrah, joined by Judge Breitenstein, distinguished inability to understand from weakness making a person susceptible to exploitation. Modern equitable principles moved away from treating every incompetent person’s agreement as absolutely void; outside guardianship, a representative or a lucid interval could permit ratification. Physical or mental weakness alone did not establish incapacity. The question was sufficient reason to understand the transaction’s nature and effect: property, disposition, recipient, and consideration, not average intelligence or sound business judgment.

A person capable of contracting but vulnerable through weakness needed proof of fraud or overreaching for that alternative theory. The challenger bore the burden at the relevant time. Experts could not simply be ignored; uncontradicted testimony deserved respect absent countervailing expert or lay evidence. But contemporaneous observations and circumstances supplied a potential counterweight, unlike opinions relying only on others’ accounts.

Here, explained lawyer-assisted negotiations, detailed execution, deliveries, weighing and sorting, scheduling, a favorable amendment, and continued documents supported the findings. Lack of incapacity discussion among family and friends, especially in Broadbent’s presence, also mattered. Positive medical testimony did not compel a finding that Darwin failed to understand what he sold, to whom, or on what terms. Supported trial findings bound the appellate court.

sections.title: The majority finds the price proof insufficient to establish exploitation
paragraphs: Valuation testimony put the property substantially above the price. The majority nevertheless relied on negotiated improvement, the finding of adequate consideration, and stock prices exceeding actual sales from 1957–1962. A substantial company dividend within the next year did not itself prove fraud. Broadbent was a director, but no proof showed relevant information unavailable to Cundick or other shareholders. Under the Wyoming law applied, a director buying a shareholder’s stock did not automatically become a fiduciary or commit fraud through nondisclosure.

The majority sustained the finding that the amended agreement was not unconscionable, unfair, or inequitable. Having found incapacity and overreaching unproved, it expressly declined to decide actual ratification. Its recital of continued performance therefore was not a holding that this sale had necessarily been ratified.

sections.title: Hill regards the medical proof and undervaluation as decisive
sections.cue: Finish with the dissent and the actual affirmance.
paragraphs: Judge Hill found the lay counterevidence trivial. Sorting sheep did not show capacity for a complex sale, and some witnesses had not observed business decision-making. The lawyer testified by deposition, so the judge had no demeanor advantage. Hill read that account as the wife and lawyer directing material acts; their capacity could not replace Darwin’s. He also faulted absence of a specific finding on capacity at the original bargain.

The 2,252 acres sold for $39,510 against an expert value of $86,189. Company interests sold for $46,750 against even the buyer’s witness’s $73,743.45 valuation and sellers’ valuations above $105,000. A $20,000 dividend became payable within a year, and Broadbent’s directorship gave access to company affairs. Hill would scrutinize weakness combined with inadequate consideration even without total incapacity or direct proof of knowledge, and would reverse with judgment for appellant.
The majority instead affirmed dismissal on September 14, 1967. Rehearing was denied October 27, a separate date. No rescission, restitution award, or new trial resulted.
